Graph and Roots of a Quadratic Polynomial

AlgebraCurvesComplex Analysis
Game: Shape a curve like a bowl with three sliders and see where it crosses the line in the middle.
How to play: Move the sliders. Green dots show the two answers; when the bowl misses the line, they jump off it, one above and one below.

Look for the math

The equation ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 has two roots, given by the quadratic formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a

The number under the square root, the discriminant D = b² − 4ac, decides what kind they are: two different real roots if D > 0, one double root if D = 0, two complex conjugate roots if D < 0. Complex roots are drawn as points above and below the axis.

The parabola and its axis

The graph is a parabola that opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0. Both roots sit on either side of the dashed line x = −b/2a through its lowest or highest point: real roots on the x-axis, complex ones on the dashed line itself, mirror images in the x-axis.

Vieta's formulas

If x₁ and x₂ are the roots, P(x) = a(x − x₁)(x − x₂), and multiplying out gives Vieta's formulas: x₁ + x₂ = −b/a and x₁x₂ = c/a. When the roots are complex, α ± βi, their product is α² + β², the square of their distance from 0. So if a and c stay fixed, the complex roots move along a circle of radius √(c/a) as b changes; the faint circle shows it. The test checked all of this on 67,240 polynomials across the sliders.

Moving c

Changing c just lifts or lowers the parabola. Start with two real roots and a > 0, and raise c: at c = b²/4a, when ax² + bx + c is a perfect square, the parabola touches the axis and the two roots meet; after that they split into a complex pair.

Set a = 1 and c = 4, then slide b from −10 to 10. Watch the roots run along the x-axis, meet, go round the circle and meet again.
